channel.title: Ryan's Daily Learning

item.title: Big Idea: Braess's Paradox — Daily Learning
item.description: Adding a road can slow everyone down, which is Braess's paradox. In the classic example, drivers chasing the fastest route for themselves turn a 65-minute trip into an 80-minute one for everyone.
item.content:encoded: Adding a road can slow everyone down, which is Braess's paradox. In the classic example, drivers chasing the fastest route for themselves turn a 65-minute trip into an 80-minute one for everyone.

item.title: Statistics: The Prosecutor's Fallacy — Daily Learning
item.description: A mammography test that usually catches cancer and sometimes flags healthy women still leaves a positive result meaning only about a 9.2% chance of cancer when the condition is rare. Most gynecologists asked got that wrong, reading the chance of a positive given cancer as the chance of cancer given a positive.

item.title: Word of the Day: parallax — Daily Learning
item.description: Parallax (PAR-uh-laks) is the apparent shift in an object's position when you look at it from two different vantage points. From the passenger seat, parallax made the speedometer needle look faster than it really was.

item.title: Statistics: The Birthday Paradox — Daily Learning
item.description: In a group of just 23 people, the chance at least two share a birthday is 50.7%. Count pairs instead of people, and the group makes 253 chances for a match.

item.title: Word of the Day: apricity - Daily Learning
item.description: Merriam-Webster's 2023 winter-words guide defines apricity (uh-PRISS-ih-tee) as a noun meaning the warmth of the sun on a cold winter's day. On a cold November morning, I stepped out of the shade and stood in the apricity for a minute before going back inside.

item.title: Big Idea: The Experience Machine — Daily Learning
item.description: In 1974, Robert Nozick imagined a machine that could stimulate your brain to give you any experience you wanted, pre-programmed two years at a time, while you floated in a tank with electrodes attached and never knew you were there. He thought most people would refuse it, calling plugging in "a kind of suicide" because we want to actually do things and be a certain kind of person.

item.title: Big Idea: The Sleeping Beauty Problem — Daily Learning
item.description: Beauty is put to sleep on Sunday and a fair coin is tossed, heads waking her on Monday only and tails waking her on Monday and Tuesday with her memory erased, so she cannot tell which waking this is. The sharpest reading is that 1/2 and 1/3 answer two different questions, the chance the coin landed heads and the chance this awakening followed heads.

item.title: Statistics: Overfitting and the Bias–Variance Tradeoff — Daily Learning
item.description: Say a betting model fitted to 200 past games nails 68% of them, then only 51% of the next 100. It chased quirks of the old sample instead of the real pattern, and that is the bias–variance tradeoff: simple models stay stable but miss real patterns, while complex ones catch more and swing with each new sample.

item.title: Word of the Day: ineluctable - Daily Learning
item.description: ineluctable (in-ih-LUK-tuh-bul) is an adjective meaning impossible to avoid or escape, inescapable, inevitable. From Latin in- (not) + eluctari (to struggle out of), it literally means “cannot be struggled out of,” as in the ineluctable pull of a deadline.

item.title: Big Idea: The Anthropic Principle — Daily Learning
item.description: The weak anthropic principle, as Britannica sets it out in an update dated November 9, 2026, says we could only ever wake up in a universe where waking up is possible. The strong version goes further, saying the universe must in some sense permit observers to exist.

item.title: Statistics: Importance Sampling — Daily Learning
item.description: When a distribution is too hard to sample from directly, importance sampling draws from an easier one instead and reweights each draw by how likely it would have been under the target, so the weighted average still answers the original question. A poker player might simulate a rare river card 10 times as often as fair dealing would produce it, then count each such hand as one-tenth as much.

item.title: Word of the Day: eristic — Daily Learning
item.description: Eristic (eh-RIS-tik) is an adjective given to arguing for the sake of argument, where winning the dispute matters more than finding the truth. The meeting started as a genuine question about the budget, but it turned eristic once winning the argument mattered more than getting the numbers right.

item.title: Big Idea: Mary's Room — Daily Learning
item.description: Frank Jackson's Knowledge Argument imagines Mary, a brilliant colour scientist who knows all the physical facts about vision yet has spent her whole life in a black-and-white room and never seen colour. When she steps out and sees a red tomato for the first time, Jackson says she learns something new, what it is like to see red, and that leaves the question of whether a machine that knew…
item.content:encoded: Frank Jackson's Knowledge Argument imagines Mary, a brilliant colour scientist who knows all the physical facts about vision yet has spent her whole life in a black-and-white room and never seen colour. When she steps out and sees a red tomato for the first time, Jackson says she learns something new, what it is like to see red, and that leaves the question of whether a machine that knew everything about a mind would know what having one feels like.

item.title: Word of the Day: quiddity — Daily Learning
item.description: Quiddity (KWID-i-tee) is a noun for the essential nature of a thing, its whatness, from Latin quidditas, from quid ("what"). The quiddity of a good poker bluff is the story it tells.

item.title: Statistics: Bootstrapping — Daily Learning
item.description: When you can't collect more data, resample the data you already have, drawing many new samples of the same size with replacement and recomputing your statistic each time. The spread of those values is your uncertainty: 100 poker sessions averaging +$12 a session might land between +$4 and +$20 in 95% of 10,000 resamples.

item.title: Big Idea: Roko's Basilisk — Daily Learning
item.description: In 2010, LessWrong user Roko proposed that a future superintelligent AI might simulate and punish anyone who knew about it but did nothing to help create it. The idea was broadly rejected because punishment after the AI exists cannot change whether it came into being.

The noctivagant fox slipped through the sleeping neighborhood long after the streetlights had flickered on, sharper than nocturnal because it captures the wandering, not just the wakefulness.

item.title: Big Idea: The St. Petersburg Paradox — Daily Learning
item.description: Flip a fair coin until it first lands tails, and if that takes n flips the prize is $2^n, so the game's expected value is infinite. Bernoulli's answer, published in 1738, was that each extra dollar is worth a little less than the one before, so the game is worth only $4.

item.title: Word of the Day: vellichor — Daily Learning
item.description: Vellichor (VEL-ih-kor) is a noun for the strange wistfulness of used bookstores, which are somehow infused with the passage of time, the sense that thousands of books once belonged to people who are now gone and their stories linger on the shelves. Stepping into the shop, I felt vellichor among the thousands of old books I would never have time to read.

item.title: Statistics: Survivorship Bias — Daily Learning
item.description: Survivorship bias is the error of drawing conclusions only from the winners who survived a process while ignoring the losers who vanished. Imagine 100 bettors try the same touted system, and only the lucky survivors are left posting their winning slips.

item.title: Statistics: p-hacking and multiple comparisons — Daily Learning
item.description: P-hacking is running analysis after analysis until one clears the bar, then reporting that p-value as if it were the only test you ran. Run 20 independent betting angles at the usual 5% threshold and roughly 64% of the time at least one will look significant by luck alone, as a May 7, 2026 explainer on the multiple-comparisons problem lays out.

item.title: Big Idea: The Prisoner's Dilemma — Daily Learning
item.description: In the Prisoner's Dilemma, betraying beats staying silent whatever the other prisoner does, so self-interest pushes both to betray even though staying silent together would serve them both better. When the game repeats, tit-for-tat can make cooperation pay by cooperating first and then copying whatever the other player did last.

item.title: Big Idea: The Sorites Paradox — Daily Learning
item.description: Revisiting the heap, one grain of sand is not a heap and a million grains clearly is, yet adding one grain to a non-heap supposedly cannot make it one. In the Sorites paradox, the fault is the vague word “heap,” which admits borderline cases and no sharp cut-off, the same looseness behind any line drawn on a gradual change.

item.description: Sempiternal (sem-pi-TER-nul) is an adjective meaning everlasting, existing forever without beginning or end in the general sense. Many debates about freedom boil down to the sempiternal question of man's responsibility to himself versus his responsibility to society.

item.title: Statistics: Calibration — Daily Learning
item.description: A bettor pricing 100 bets at 60% should win about 60 of them, so 45 wins means the price was too high. Checking it means sorting predictions into buckets by the probability you stated and comparing each bucket's actual hit rate with its stated number, to see whether you are calibrated.

item.title: Statistics: Expected Value of Information — Daily Learning
item.description: Information is worth only what it changes about your decision: if learning the answer would leave your action the same, it has no decision value for that choice. On a $50 call with a 40% chance of winning a $150 pot, a perfect read would be worth $30 on average, so a tell or solver study costing more than that is a skip.

item.title: Word of the Day: ultracrepidarian — Daily Learning
item.description: Ultracrepidarian (ul-truh-krep-i-DAIR-ee-un) is an adjective, also used as a noun, for someone who gives opinions on a subject they know little or nothing about. The story goes that the painter Apelles, listening unseen as a cobbler rightly faulted a sandal with too few loops in his painting, fixed it, then told the emboldened cobbler, who moved on to criticising the subject's leg, not to judge…

item.title: Big Idea: The Raven Paradox — Daily Learning
item.description: In the raven paradox, “all ravens are black” is logically equivalent to “all non-black things are non-ravens,” so a white shoe counts as evidence for a claim about ravens. Under Bayesian thinking, a black raven tells you far more than a white shoe, because ravens are rare and non-black things are everywhere.

item.description: Palimpsest (PAL-im-sest) is a noun for a manuscript page scraped clean and written over again, with traces of the earlier writing still showing through. A mind can be one too, a palimpsest of everything it has absorbed.

item.title: Big Idea: The Doomsday Argument — Daily Learning
item.description: If you count yourself as a randomly drawn human from everyone who will ever live, the Bayesian version puts humanity's total under 2 trillion. The catch is that merely existing favors worlds with far more humans, so your rank may not be the random draw the math assumes.

item.title: Statistics: Hierarchical Models and Partial Pooling — Daily Learning
item.description: Partial pooling pulls each group's estimate partway toward the overall average instead of judging groups alone or lumping them together, with the pull hardest for small samples. A rookie who went 2-for-3, at 67%, might land near 50% against a 45% team average while a veteran with 400 attempts barely moves, so an early hot streak should not be taken at face value.

item.title: Statistics: Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) — Daily Learning
item.description: When a posterior is too tangled to calculate directly, a random walk can map it, the way you would map a dark room, by where you spend the most time. A proposed spot is accepted with probability equal to its probability divided by the current spot's, capped at one, so a spot half as likely is taken half the time.

item.title: Big Idea: The Ship of Theseus — Daily Learning
item.description: The Athenians kept Theseus's thirty-oared ship afloat by swapping each decaying plank for new timber until none of the original wood remained. The discarded planks rebuilt into a second ship pose the same question as a mind rebuilt neuron by neuron, whether sameness lives in the pattern or in the material.

item.title: Word of the Day: oneiric
item.description: Oneiric means relating to dreams or dreaming. The foggy morning street felt oneiric, quiet and half-lit, as if I were still dreaming.

item.title: Statistics: Likelihood Ratios — Daily Learning
item.description: A likelihood ratio is the probability of seeing a piece of evidence if a hypothesis is true, divided by the probability of seeing it if the hypothesis is false. A player who bets big on the river 80% of the time with the nuts but only 20% of the time when bluffing gives that bet a likelihood ratio of 4, so Bayes' rule in odds form multiplies your prior odds that they have it by four.

item.title: Big Idea: The Chinese Room — Daily Learning
item.description: In 1980 John Searle imagined himself locked in a room in the Chinese Room, following an English rulebook to return perfect Chinese answers without understanding a word of Chinese. If a machine can pass every test of understanding by following rules for symbols without grasping what they mean, how would we ever tell the difference?

item.title: Statistics: Credible vs. Confidence Intervals — Daily Learning
item.description: After a quarterback's first 40 throws, a model might put his true completion rate between 58% and 68%, and as a 95% credible interval that means you are 95% sure his true rate is in there. The confidence interval from the same data can look identical on paper, yet it answers a different question: if you repeated the procedure many times, about 95% of the intervals it produced would contain the…

The confidence interval from the same data can look identical on paper, yet it answers a different question: if you repeated the procedure many times, about 95% of the intervals it produced would contain the true value.

item.title: Big Idea: The Simulation Argument — Daily Learning
item.description: Nick Bostrom's 2003 argument is that a posthuman civilization could run so many detailed simulations of conscious minds that the simulated would vastly outnumber the real. That leaves three options: humanity goes extinct before reaching that stage, posthumans almost never run such simulations, or we are almost certainly living in one.

item.description: Liminal, pronounced LIM-ih-nul, is an adjective for a transitional, in-between state. That strange quiet hour between finishing a project and starting the next is a liminal one.

item.title: Big Idea: The Gettier Problem — Daily Learning
item.description: In June 1963, Edmund Gettier argued in a three-page paper that justified true belief is not enough for knowledge. Smith had good reason to believe the man who would get the job had ten coins in his pocket, yet he was right only because he himself got the job and had ten coins himself.

item.title: Anodyne: too bland to object to
item.description: Anodyne (AN-uh-dyne) is, per Merriam-Webster, not likely to offend or arouse tensions, and as a noun it is something that soothes pain. "The otherwise anodyne comments sounded quite inflammatory when taken out of context" shows the useful distinction: it is merely too bland to object to, not genuinely harmless.

item.title: Statistics: Publication Bias - Daily Learning
item.description: Publication bias, as Scribbr defined it in October 2022, is what happens when exciting, positive results get published while null or boring ones stay unpublished in a drawer, the file-drawer problem. Imagine 20 labs test a useless betting system and, by chance, one finds a “significant” edge, and only that study gets published, so readers see a system that works.

item.title: Statistics: The Kelly Criterion — Daily Learning
item.description: The Kelly criterion sizes a bet from your edge and the odds, so a 55% chance at even money calls for 10% of your bankroll. Because that 55% is only an estimate, half-Kelly keeps about 75% of the growth while roughly halving the swings.

item.title: Big Idea: The Grandfather Paradox — Daily Learning
item.description: If you go back before your grandfather has children and stop him from having any, you are never born, so nobody goes back to stop him. The ways out are a fixed timeline, where the attempt must fail, or a branching one, where you arrive in a timeline without you.

item.title: Big Idea: The Ultimatum Game — Daily Learning
item.description: In a 2009 paper on experiments around the world, one player proposes a split of $100 and the other can reject it and leave both with nothing, yet people routinely reject offers below roughly 20–30% rather than accept an unfair split. What is the smallest split you would accept, and what does that number say about you?

item.title: Word of the Day: sonder — Daily Learning
item.description: In Holstee's 2018 account, sonder (noun, pronounced SON-der, rhymes with ponder) is the sudden realization that each random passerby is living a life as vivid and complex as your own, with their own ambitions, friendships, routines, and worries, just as real as yours. “Stuck in airport traffic, I had a moment of sonder watching the driver in the next lane sing along to the radio, suddenly aware…
item.content:encoded: In Holstee's 2018 account, sonder (noun, pronounced SON-der, rhymes with ponder) is the sudden realization that each random passerby is living a life as vivid and complex as your own, with their own ambitions, friendships, routines, and worries, just as real as yours. “Stuck in airport traffic, I had a moment of sonder watching the driver in the next lane sing along to the radio, suddenly aware of the whole invisible life behind that windshield.”

item.title: Statistics: The Prosecutor's Fallacy — Daily Learning
item.description: The prosecutor's fallacy is confusing the chance of seeing this evidence if someone were innocent with the chance they are innocent given that evidence. A 1-in-a-million DNA match sounds like near-certain guilt, but in a city of 10 million you would expect about 10 innocent matches by chance alone.
